subject: surgery
title: Cleft Palate and Acute Hand Infections: Paronychia and Felon

steps.tx: Embryological development of the secondary palate involves the elevation, horizontal migration, and midline fusion of the paired lateral palatine processes of the maxillary prominences between the seventh and twelfth weeks of gestation. Failure of these palatal shelves to unite with each other and the nasal septum produces a **cleft palate**. The defect may range from a submucous cleft or isolated bifid uvula to complete clefting of both the soft and hard palate extending forward to the incisive foramen.
steps.say: Cleft palate arises from failed fusion of the secondary palatal shelves during early embryonic life. Defects range from an isolated bifid uvula to complete clefting extending through the hard palate.

vis.alt: Medical diagram illustrating craniofacial clefting and structural palate deformities.
vis.caption: Anatomical disruption of the hard and soft palate in congenital orofacial cleft syndromes. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Unrepaired palatal clefts inflict substantial functional morbidity, impairing infantile feeding because the infant cannot create an airtight intraoral seal to generate negative suction. Disruption of the tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini muscle sling leads to persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction, predisposing virtually all affected children to chronic recurrent serous otitis media and conductive hearing loss. As speech develops, failure of the soft palate to close against the posterior pharyngeal wall causes severe **velopharyngeal insufficiency**, producing hypernasal resonance and compensatory articulation errors.
steps.say: Children with unrepaired palatal clefts cannot generate intraoral suction for feeding and develop chronic otitis media from Eustachian tube dysfunction. Velopharyngeal insufficiency causes severe hypernasal speech.

rows: Infant Feeding
Inability to generate intraoral negative suction
Requires specialized squeeze bottles (Haberman feeder)
Middle Ear Function
Tensor veli palatini failure to open Eustachian tube
Recurrent serous otitis media; mandates tympanostomy grommets
Speech Development
Velopharyngeal sphincter incompetence
Hypernasal speech and compensatory pharyngeal fricatives
Maxillofacial Growth
Scarring from early palatoplasty
Midface hypoplasia and Class III malocclusion

steps.tx: Determining the timing of palatoplasty balances speech development needs against potential midfacial skeletal growth restriction. Surgical closure of the palate is performed between nine and eighteen months of age, ideally before the child begins developing intelligible speech patterns, while minimizing surgical scarring that could restrict subsequent maxillary anteroposterior growth. Standard surgical techniques like the **two-flap palatoplasty** of Bardach or the pushback palatoplasty incorporate meticulous intravelar veloplasty, surgically detaching the abnormally oriented levator veli palatini muscles from the posterior hard palate to reconstruct a functional retroclinal muscular sling.
steps.say: Palatoplasty is ideally performed between nine and eighteen months to facilitate normal speech while minimizing maxillary growth restriction. Intravelar veloplasty reconstructs the essential levator muscle sling.

nodes.label: Intravelar Veloplasty to Realign Levator Muscles

steps.tx: Transitioning to acute surgical emergencies of the upper extremity, closed fascial compartments of the hand make infections particularly destructive. The most frequently encountered superficial infection is acute **paronychia**, which affects the soft tissue fold surrounding the nail plate. Typically initiated by minor trauma such as nail-biting, aggressive manicures, or hangnail pulling, Staphylococcus aureus invades the lateral nail fold. Infection produces intense throbbing pain, localized erythema, and marked oedema bordering the lateral margin of the nail.
steps.say: Acute paronychia is a common infection of the lateral nail fold, typically caused by staphylococcal invasion following minor cuticle trauma. Patients present with throbbing pain, redness, and localized swelling.

nodes.label: Elevate Eponychial Fold or Partial Nail Plate Excision

steps.tx: Management of acute paronychia depends strictly on the clinical stage of presentation. In the early cellulitic phase without demonstrable fluctuance, conservative measures comprising warm water soaks, hand elevation, and targeted oral antistaphylococcal antibiotics achieve resolution. Once a localized abscess forms beneath the eponychium, surgical drainage is mandatory. Drainage entails gently inserting the tip of an eleven-blade scalpel or iris scissors beneath the lateral nail fold to release the trapped pus without incising the germinal nail matrix, followed by partial **nail avulsion** if purulence tracks subungually.
steps.say: Early paronychia responds to warm soaks and antibiotics, but formed collections require drainage. Lifting the eponychial fold releases the pus, and underlying subungual extension mandates partial nail removal.

right.title: Fluctuant Abscess / Runaround
points: Pus tracking beneath the nail bed
Mandates partial or complete nail plate avulsion

steps.tx: The fingertip here is swollen drum-tight, with pus pointing through the pulp where fibrous septa trap pressure against bone. This **felon** throbs relentlessly because its closed compartments cannot expand, threatening the distal phalanx and flexor sheath if drainage waits. Unlike surface paronychia around the nail, pulp infection needs a decompression incision that respects digital nerves and vessels.
steps.say: A drum-tight pointing fingertip pulp indicates a felon trapped by fibrous septa. Timely decompression protects bone and flexor sheath.

steps.tx: Infection involving the closed anatomical terminal pulp space of the distal digit is termed a **felon** or whitlow. The distal digital pulp is compartmentalized into numerous small, non-compliant fibrofatty chambers by tough vertical fibrous septa that anchor the deep dermis to the underlying periosteum of the distal phalanx. Typically inoculated by minor puncture wounds from splinters or needles, bacterial proliferation within these enclosed fibrous chambers triggers a rapid increase in compartment pressure, compromising microvascular capillary perfusion.
steps.say: A felon is a closed pulp space infection of the terminal digit. Rigid vertical fibrous septa connect the skin to bone, creating high-pressure compartments where swelling can induce ischaemic tissue necrosis.

rows: Anatomical Location
Lateral nail fold and eponychial margin
Volar closed fibrofatty pulp space of distal phalanx
Primary Risk Factor
Nail biting, manicuring, hangnail picking
Minor puncture wound (wooden splinter, sewing needle)
Key Complication
Subungual abscess and chronic nail dystrophy
Digital artery thrombosis and distal phalanx osteomyelitis
Incision Approach
Sulcus elevation or partial nail plate removal
Mid-lateral or direct longitudinal incision over fluctuance

steps.tx: Unrelieved compartment pressure within the terminal digital pulp rapidly causes digital capillary occlusion and ischaemic necrosis of the pulp tissues. Furthermore, because several fibrous septa insert directly onto the periosteum, untreated infections frequently spread directly to the underlying bone, resulting in destructive **osteomyelitis** of the distal phalanx. Patients present with severe, agonizingly throbbing pain, tense swelling, and exquisite tenderness localized to the volar digital pad, unable to sleep due to pulsating discomfort.
steps.say: High compartment pressure in a felon can thrombose digital capillaries and cause distal phalanx osteomyelitis. Patients experience agonizing throbbing pain and tense swelling of the fingertip pad.

nodes.label: Emergency Incision and Drainage to Prevent Osteomyelitis

steps.tx: Emergency surgical drainage is required whenever tense induration or fluctuance develops in a felon. The optimal surgical technique utilizes a direct longitudinal volar incision placed strictly over the point of maximal fluctuance, or a **mid-axial incision** along the non-working lateral border of the digit, positioned dorsal to the neurovascular bundle. The surgeon divides the tense vertical fibrous septa to ensure uninhibited drainage while avoiding deep exploration that might contaminate the sterile flexor tendon sheath or injure the digital nerve.
steps.say: Surgical drainage requires dividing the vertical fibrous septa over the point of fluctuance or via a mid-lateral approach. Careful dissection avoids damaging the digital nerve or entering the flexor tendon sheath.

rows: Longitudinal Volar Incision
Directly over maximal fluctuance on tactile pad
Avoids crossing distal flexion crease; highly effective
Mid-Axial Lateral Incision
Non-touch lateral border dorsal to digital bundle
Spares volar tactile sensation; technically meticulous
Fishmouth Incision
Transverse incision around entire fingertip margin
Historical technique now condemned due to unstable scar
Through-and-Through
Bilateral incisions with drain passed through
Condemned due to excessive scarring and anaesthetic fingertip
